cards.front: The kidney's ledger for one substance: excreted = filtered − {{c1::reabsorbed}} + secreted.
cards.back: What leaves in urine is what was filtered, minus what the tubules took back, plus what they added.
cards.quote: What leaves in urine is what the kidney filtered, minus what its tubules took back, plus what they added: excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.

cards.front: In the mammalian kidney, why does the take-back (reabsorption), not the filter, largely set how much water leaves in urine?
cards.back: The kidney filters far more than it lets go: an adult human filters about 180 L of plasma a day and takes back about 99% of the water.
cards.why: With filtration that large, the share taken back decides how much is left over as urine.
cards.quote: Because the kidney filters far more than it lets go, the take-back, not the filter, largely sets how much water you lose.

cards.front: How does water taken back by the kidney tubule cross the tubule wall?
cards.back: Passively, mainly by osmosis down gradients that solute transport creates: mostly salt, and deep in the kidney also urea. No pump moves water.
cards.quote: No pump moves water across the tubule wall: water taken back moves passively, mainly by osmosis down gradients that solute transport creates

cards.front: At the glomerulus, what moves water into the filtrate, and how does that differ from water reabsorption along the tubule?
cards.back: Starling forces push water through the filter in bulk. Along the tubule, water moves by osmosis down gradients made by solute transport.
cards.quote: at the glomerulus, Starling forces push water through the filter in bulk

cards.front: Trace blood through the vessels that serve one mammalian nephron.
cards.back: Afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries around the tube (and, for nephrons reaching deep into the kidney, the vasa recta).
cards.quote: Blood enters and leaves the glomerulus by the afferent and efferent arterioles (afferent in, efferent out)
cards.section: Where each term happens

cards.front: Trace filtrate through a mammalian nephron, from where it forms to the last stretch.
cards.back: Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule → loop of Henle (descending, then ascending limb) → distal tubule → collecting duct, which many nephrons share.
cards.quote: The filtrate then flows through four stretches, the last shared by many nephrons.
cards.section: Where each term happens

cards.front: The mammalian proximal tubule takes back about {{c1::60 to 70%}} of filtered sodium, with water following so the fluid stays near plasma's concentration.
cards.back: It also takes back almost all filtered glucose and amino acids.
cards.quote: About 60 to 70% of filtered sodium, with water following so the fluid stays at nearly plasma's concentration
cards.section: Where each term happens

cards.front: In the mammalian collecting duct, what do principal cells and intercalated cells each handle?
cards.back: Principal cells: take back sodium and secrete potassium. Intercalated cells: secrete acid or bicarbonate (acid-base balance).
cards.quote: Potassium (principal cells); acid or bicarbonate (intercalated cells, part of acid-base balance, gas exchange)
cards.section: Where each term happens

cards.front: Which parts of the mammalian nephron set the final water and salt content of urine under hormonal control?
cards.back: The late distal tubule and the collecting duct.
cards.quote: The late distal tubule and the collecting duct set the final water and salt content of urine under hormonal control.
cards.section: Where each term happens

cards.front: Micropuncture of frog kidneys (1924): fluid drawn from Bowman's capsule held sugar and chloride but no detectable protein, while bladder urine held no sugar. What does this show?
cards.back: The first step is a filter (small solutes pass, protein does not), followed by reabsorption of sugar along the tubule, in the frog.
cards.why: It did not say where along the tubule or give mammalian rates; frog nephrons lack a loop of Henle.
cards.quote: It held sugar and chloride but no protein their tests could find; the frog's bladder urine held no sugar.
cards.section: Micropuncture: is the first step really a filter?

cards.front: Suppose the glomerulus supplied mostly water and tubule cells secreted the solutes of urine. What would fluid sampled from Bowman's capsule lack, and what comparison in the same animal would show reabsorption instead?
cards.back: It would lack plasma solutes such as sugar. Compare capsule fluid with bladder urine: a solute present in the capsule but absent from the bladder was taken back.
cards.quote: A rival camp held that the glomerulus supplies mostly water and tubule cells secrete the solutes of urine.
cards.section: Micropuncture: is the first step really a filter?

cards.front: What is renal clearance, and how is it calculated?
cards.back: C = U × V / P: the volume of plasma that would hold the amount excreted each minute. No plasma is really wiped clean.
cards.why: U × V is the excretion rate (urine concentration times urine flow); P is plasma concentration.
cards.quote: Divide by plasma concentration P and you get the volume of plasma that would hold that much each minute: the clearance.
cards.section: Clearance: reading the ledger from outside

cards.front: Why does inulin clearance equal the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
cards.back: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so excreted equals filtered, and its clearance is the plasma volume filtered per minute.
cards.quote: Inulin, a plant sugar polymer, is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so excreted equals filtered
cards.section: Clearance: reading the ledger from outside

cards.front: An adult human at steady state produces 90 mL of urine in 45 min. Inulin is 25 mg per mL in urine and 0.40 mg per mL in plasma. What is the GFR, and how much plasma is filtered per day?
cards.back: V = 90 / 45 = 2.0 mL per min. C = U × V / P = 25 × 2.0 / 0.40 = 125 mL per min = GFR. Per day: 125 × 1,440 = 180,000 mL, about 180 L.
cards.quote: 120 mL of urine in 60 min gives V = 2.0 mL per min.
cards.section: Worked problem: clearance and filtered load

cards.front: GFR is 125 mL per min and plasma glucose is 6.0 mmol per L. What is the filtered load of glucose per minute and per day? If no glucose appears in the urine, how much was reabsorbed?
cards.back: Filtered load = GFR × P = 0.125 L per min × 6.0 mmol per L = 0.75 mmol per min; × 1,440 = 1,080 mmol per day. With none in urine, all of it was reabsorbed.
cards.why: Glucose is freely filtered, so filtered load is GFR times plasma concentration.
cards.quote: filtered load = GFR x P = 0.120 L per min x 5.0 mmol per L = 0.60 mmol per min
cards.section: Worked problem: clearance and filtered load

cards.front: For a freely filtered substance, what does a clearance above GFR mean, and what does one far below GFR mean?
cards.back: Above GFR: net secretion (it leaves faster than filtration alone could carry it). Far below GFR: it is mostly reabsorbed.
cards.quote: For a freely filtered substance, a clearance above GFR means net secretion
cards.section: Worked problem: clearance and filtered load

cards.front: GFR is 120 mL per min. A freely filtered substance has plasma concentration 1.0 mg per mL, urine concentration 40 mg per mL, and urine flow 1.0 mL per min. Find its filtered load, excretion rate, clearance and net tubular handling.
cards.back: Filtered = 120 × 1.0 = 120 mg per min. Excreted = 40 × 1.0 = 40 mg per min. Clearance = 40 mL per min. Net reabsorbed = 120 − 40 = 80 mg per min.
cards.why: Ledger: excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted; clearance below GFR means net reabsorption.
cards.quote: Urine concentration U times urine flow V is the excretion rate
cards.section: Clearance: reading the ledger from outside

cards.front: GFR is 120 mL per min. A freely filtered drug has plasma concentration 0.10 mg per mL, urine concentration 20 mg per mL, and urine flow 1.5 mL per min. What is its clearance, and how does the tubule handle it?
cards.back: C = 20 × 1.5 / 0.10 = 300 mL per min, above GFR, so net secretion. Filtered 12 mg per min, excreted 30 mg per min: about 18 mg per min secreted on net.
cards.quote: at 300 mL per min the substance leaves faster than filtration alone could carry it
cards.section: Worked problem: clearance and filtered load

cards.front: Creatinine clearance is used to estimate GFR. Why does it tend to overestimate GFR?
cards.back: A little creatinine is secreted by the tubule, so more leaves in urine than filtration alone delivers.
cards.quote: Creatinine, a muscle waste, is used to estimate GFR, but a little is secreted, so creatinine clearance tends to overestimate GFR.
cards.section: Worked problem: clearance and filtered load

cards.front: Adult human plasma is about 290 mOsm per kg; a water-deprived adult can make urine near {{c1::1,200}} mOsm per kg.
cards.back: Osmolality counts dissolved particles per kilogram of water.
cards.quote: adult human plasma is about 290 mOsm per kg (osmolality, dissolved particles per kilogram of water); a water-deprived adult can make urine near 1,200.
cards.section: Making urine more concentrated than blood

cards.front: How does the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle build the outer medulla's osmotic gradient?
cards.back: It moves sodium chloride out of the tubule (mainly through the NKCC2 cotransporter, powered by the sodium-potassium pump) while staying nearly impermeable to water, so salt leaves without water.
cards.quote: The thick ascending limb takes up sodium chloride mainly through a cotransporter called NKCC2, with the sodium-potassium pump supplying the energy.
cards.section: Testing each limb on its own

cards.front: In an idealized outer-medullary loop of Henle, salt transport per level, flow, wall leakiness and blood washout are held fixed while the loop is made twice as long. What happens to the deepest tissue's osmolality, and why?
cards.back: It can end up more concentrated: a longer countercurrent path gives the modest difference at each level more steps to add up. This is a direction, not a number.
cards.why: Real long loops also reach the inner medulla, whose mechanism is unresolved.
cards.quote: a longer countercurrent path gives the difference more steps to add up
cards.section: Why a modest difference adds up

cards.front: Single thin descending limbs from rabbit kidneys were held between glass pipettes and perfused (isolated perfused tubule method). Sodium permeability was low and no active salt transport was detected. What does this imply about how the descending limb's fluid changes?
cards.back: No active salt transport was detected in the rabbit descending limb; it gives up water to the concentrated medulla, so its fluid concentrates by losing water.
cards.why: In rats, some inner-medullary descending segments lack aquaporin-1, so this is not true of every segment in every species.
cards.quote: Sodium permeability was low, and no active salt transport could be detected.
cards.section: Testing each limb on its own

cards.front: How do the vasa recta remove reabsorbed water without washing out the medullary gradient?
cards.back: They run in hairpins: blood going down gains salt and loses water, and blood coming up does the reverse. Blood leaves with the water but little of the salt (countercurrent exchange).
cards.quote: So blood leaves carrying reabsorbed water but little of the salt: this countercurrent exchange limits washout of the gradient.
cards.section: Keeping the gradient

cards.front: In the inner medulla, how does urea leave the collecting duct and what does it contribute?
cards.back: Through urea transporters, by facilitated diffusion (not an active pump); it adds to the inner medulla's osmotic gradient.
cards.quote: urea leaves the collecting duct through urea transporters, by facilitated diffusion rather than an active pump
cards.section: The inner medulla, and urine without ADH

cards.front: Without antidiuretic hormone (ADH), why is urine dilute rather than merely plasma-strength?
cards.back: The thick ascending limb has already removed salt without water, and a collecting duct mostly closed to water keeps the fluid dilute.
cards.quote: Without ADH, urine is dilute, not merely plasma-strength
cards.section: The inner medulla, and urine without ADH

cards.front: A water-deprived mammal with high ADH is given a drug that blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Predict the medullary osmolality and the urine osmolality, and explain why high ADH cannot rescue concentration.
cards.back: Medullary osmolality falls and urine osmolality moves toward plasma's. ADH opens the collecting duct to water, but water leaves only down a gradient, and the salt transport that builds the gradient is blocked.
cards.why: Combines the thick ascending limb's salt-without-water rule with passive water movement in the collecting duct.
cards.quote: the thick ascending limb has already removed salt without water
cards.section: The inner medulla, and urine without ADH

cards.front: After heavy sweating, a person's plasma osmolality rises. Predict the ADH response and the effect on urine volume and concentration.
cards.back: ADH release rises; collecting-duct water reabsorption rises, so urine is smaller in volume and more concentrated.
cards.why: ADH is released when plasma osmolality rises or blood volume falls.
cards.quote: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: In collecting-duct cells, through which receptor, second messenger and water channel does ADH act?
cards.back: V2 receptors, cAMP, and aquaporin-2 water channels.
cards.quote: In collecting-duct cells it acts through V2 receptors and cAMP (G proteins, cAMP and PKA).
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: In perfused rat collecting ducts, vasopressin raises water permeability within minutes, and the rise reverses on washout. What labeling result for aquaporin-2 would show that vasopressin moves stored channels rather than making new ones?
cards.back: More apical-membrane labeling and less labeling in vesicles just beneath it with vasopressin, both reversing on washout: channels shuttle between stored vesicles and the apical membrane.
cards.quote: Its water channels are aquaporin-2 (Nielsen and colleagues, 1995, in perfused rat ducts).
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: Which cells release renin, and what three signals trigger release?
cards.back: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole wall. Triggers: falling renal perfusion pressure, less salt reaching the macula densa, and sympathetic stimulation of beta-adrenergic receptors.
cards.quote: Renin, an enzyme, is released by juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole when renal perfusion pressure falls
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: Give the chain from angiotensinogen to angiotensin II, naming each enzyme.
cards.back: Angiotensinogen (a plasma protein from the liver) → renin → angiotensin I → angiotensin-converting enzyme → angiotensin II.
cards.quote: Renin cuts angiotensinogen, a plasma protein made by the liver, into angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme turns that into angiotensin II.
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: How does aldosterone change sodium and potassium handling in the collecting duct?
cards.back: It raises sodium reabsorption through ENaC channels in principal cells and, coupled to that, potassium secretion.
cards.why: Aldosterone is a steroid from the adrenal cortex, released when angiotensin II stimulates it.
cards.quote: a steroid that raises sodium reabsorption through ENaC channels in principal cells and, coupled to it, potassium secretion
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: A drug blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme. Predict the effect on angiotensin II, aldosterone, and urinary sodium.
cards.back: Angiotensin II falls, so aldosterone release falls and tubular sodium reabsorption falls: more sodium leaves in urine.
cards.why: Angiotensin II raises tubular sodium reabsorption and stimulates aldosterone release.
cards.quote: Angiotensin II raises sodium reabsorption in the tubule and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: An adrenal tumor secretes excess aldosterone. Predict how urinary sodium and urinary potassium change.
cards.back: Urinary sodium falls (more reabsorbed through ENaC) and urinary potassium rises (secretion coupled to sodium reabsorption).
cards.quote: Angiotensin II raises sodium reabsorption in the tubule and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: What releases atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), and how does it change the kidney's ledger?
cards.back: Stretch of the atria (as after a rise in blood volume). It raises GFR, suppresses renin and aldosterone, and lowers sodium and water reabsorption (in rat experiments): more sodium and water in urine.
cards.quote: It raises GFR and suppresses the release of renin and aldosterone.
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: A large volume of plasma-strength saline is infused into a healthy adult, raising blood volume without changing plasma osmolality. Predict the direction of ANP, renin and ADH, and the net effect on urine.
cards.back: ANP rises; renin (and so angiotensin II and aldosterone) falls; ADH falls or does not rise. More sodium and water are excreted.
cards.why: ANP answers atrial stretch; renin answers falling pressure or salt; ADH answers rising osmolality or falling volume, neither present here.
cards.quote: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), from heart muscle cells of the stretched atria (as after a rise in blood volume), pushes the other way.
cards.section: Hormones tune the reabsorbed term

cards.front: Which vertebrates have loops of Henle, and which make urine more concentrated than their plasma?
cards.back: Only mammals and birds, on both counts. Amphibians and most fish have no loop; their urine is at most about as concentrated as their plasma.
cards.quote: Among vertebrates, loops of Henle occur only in mammals and birds, and only these make urine more concentrated than their plasma.
cards.section: Kidneys compared: the ledger in other animals

cards.front: Across many mammal species, which kidney feature tracks maximum urine concentration, and how does the kangaroo rat fit?
cards.back: Relative medullary thickness. The desert kangaroo rat has long loops and a thick inner medulla and makes urine several times more concentrated than an adult human can.
cards.quote: Across many mammal species, Beuchat (1990) found that relative medullary thickness tracks maximum urine concentration.
cards.section: Kidneys compared: the ledger in other animals

cards.front: A mammal must excrete 900 mOsm of solute. How much urine water does that take at plasma's level (about 300 mOsm per kg), at the human maximum (about 1,200), and at four times the human maximum (4,800)?
cards.back: Water = load / urine concentration: 900 / 300 = 3.0 L; 900 / 1,200 = 0.75 L; 900 / 4,800 ≈ 0.19 L.
cards.quote: load divided by the concentration the kidney can reach
cards.section: Kidneys compared: the ledger in other animals

cards.front: Birds concentrate urine only modestly. How do they still save water when excreting nitrogen?
cards.back: Much of their nitrogen leaves as uric acid, which takes little water.
cards.why: Birds have a mix of loopless and looped nephrons, reaching only a small multiple of plasma osmolality.
cards.quote: much of their nitrogen leaves as uric acid, which takes little water
cards.section: Kidneys compared: the ledger in other animals

cards.front: In an aglomerular marine teleost (such as the goosefish), a drug blocks the tubule cells' secretion of magnesium and sulfate into the tubule. Predict the effect on urine flow.
cards.back: Urine flow should fall (not necessarily stop, since other secreted ions may remain). With no glomeruli, filtered is zero, so urine forms only by secretion of ions with water following; blocking secretion removes some of what draws water in.
cards.quote: On the ledger, filtered is zero: everything in their urine reached the tubule by secretion.
cards.section: Kidneys compared: the ledger in other animals

cards.front: Two mammal species of similar size are compared; one has much greater relative medullary thickness and longer loops. Predict which is expected to reach the higher maximum urine osmolality, and which needs less water to excrete the same solute load.
cards.back: The thicker-medulla species tends to reach the higher maximum and so tends to need less water, since water needed = solute load / urine concentration reached.
cards.why: Combines the cross-species link between medullary thickness and maximum concentration with the load-over-concentration rule.
cards.quote: Across many mammal species, Beuchat (1990) found that relative medullary thickness tracks maximum urine concentration.
cards.section: Kidneys compared: the ledger in other animals

cards.front: Mice lacking the collecting-duct urea transporters UT-A1 and UT-A3 are water-restricted on a 20% and a 4% protein diet. Predict on which diet their concentrating deficit is larger, and why.
cards.back: On 20% protein: knockouts concentrated less, and the gap almost vanished on 4%. Low protein supplies little urea in either genotype, so the transporters matter little there.
cards.why: Urea comes from protein breakdown; if urea leaving the collecting duct adds to the gradient, losing that exit costs most when urea is plentiful.
cards.quote: If urea leaving the inner-medullary collecting duct adds to the gradient, knockouts should concentrate less, most on high protein
cards.section: Design problem (optional, harder)

cards.front: The passive model says urea leaving the collecting duct helps draw salt out of the thin ascending limb. UT-A1/UT-A3 knockout mice had inner-medullary NaCl not significantly different from controls but less inner-medullary urea. What do these results argue?
cards.back: They argue against the passive model's dependence on urea (it predicts less NaCl). The deficit fits less urea build-up in the inner medulla and urea trapped in the duct holding water in urine (osmotic diuresis).
cards.why: These are mice, and one knockout does not settle how the inner medulla concentrates.
cards.quote: The passive model predicts less inner-medullary NaCl in knockouts; they did not have less, which argues against that dependency.
cards.section: Design problem (optional, harder)

cards.front: Which particles actually draw water across a tubule wall?
cards.back: Those that cannot cross that wall freely (effective osmolality). While water flows, the tissue need be only slightly more concentrated than the urine.
cards.quote: what draws water across a wall is the particles that cannot cross that wall freely (effective osmolality)
cards.section: Which particles draw water
